t: Random Pick with Blacklist — Virtual Remapping
o: We must return a uniformly random integer from [0, n-1] excluding the blacklisted values, while minimizing calls to the random function. The naive idea — keep picking until we hit a non-blacklisted number (rejection sampling) — can be catastrophically slow when most of the range is blacklisted. A better idea: there are exactly $m = n - |blacklist|$ valid numbers, so a single random call in $[0, m)$ suffices if we can map each such index to a valid value in $O(1)$. Walk through Example 1: n=7, blacklist=[2,3,5], so m=4 and valid values are {0,1,4,6}; pick() draws r in [0,4) and returns the r-th smallest valid value. Constraints ($n$ up to $10^9$, up to $10^5$ blacklisted entries, $2 	imes 10^4$ picks) rule out storing all n values or looping per pick; preprocessing of size O(|blacklist| log |blacklist|) is fine.
k: There are m = n - len(blacklist) valid answers, so one uniform draw in [0, m) is enough.
Remap: for any x < m that is blacklisted, answer with some whitelisted value >= m instead, giving a bijection between [0, m) and the valid set.
Only blacklisted values below m need remapping; use a hash map built via two pointers over sorted halves.

a.i: Keep drawing uniform integers in [0, n-1) until the drawn value is not blacklisted. Each draw succeeds with probability m/n, so expected draws is n/m. This is simple but degrades badly when the blacklist covers most of the range, and it may make many random calls per pick().
s: Store the blacklist in a hash set at construction time.
On each pick(), loop: draw x = rand(n).
If x is not in the set, return it; otherwise repeat.
a.t: O(|blacklist|) preprocessing; each pick() makes an expected n/m random draws and set lookups, worst case unbounded.

a.i: Precompute the sorted array of all valid (whitelisted) values, then pick a random index into it and binary search... actually just index directly. Building the whitelist costs O(n), which is too slow for n up to 10^9, so this only works when n is small — included here as a stepping stone showing why we need virtual remapping.
s: Build the whitelist by scanning [0, n) and skipping blacklisted values.
a.t: O(n + |blacklist|) preprocessing, O(1) per pick with one random call — but O(n) memory/time is prohibitive for large n.

a.i: Let m = n - |blacklist|. Draw r uniformly in [0, m); if r itself is not blacklisted, return r. If r is blacklisted, return its mapped partner: a whitelisted value taken from the tail region [m, n). Since the number of blacklisted values below m equals the number of whitelisted values at or above m, a greedy two-pointer matching builds a perfect bijection. Only blacklisted keys need to be stored in the map, keeping memory O(|blacklist|).
s: Compute m = n - len(blacklist); sort the blacklist.
Split into B1 = blacklisted values < m and W2 = whitelisted values >= m (found by walking candidate values from m upward, skipping blacklisted ones using a pointer into the sorted blacklist).
Build map[x] = next unused element of W2 for every x in B1.
pick(): draw r = rand(m); return map[r] if present, else r.
a.t: O(B log B) preprocessing where B = |blacklist| (sorting dominates); O(1) per pick with exactly one random call.
a.sp: O(B) for the hash map and auxiliary structures.

w: In an interview, mention rejection sampling first to show intuition, then immediately note its failure mode when the blacklist dominates, and land on the hash-map remapping approach as the answer — it uses one random call per pick and O(|blacklist|) space regardless of n. Common pitfalls: forgetting that only blacklisted values strictly below m need remapping (values >= m are already valid outputs); failing to skip blacklisted values inside the tail region [m, n) when assigning partners; and off-by-one errors on the half-open ranges. Edge cases: empty blacklist (map stays empty, pick returns rand(n)), blacklist covering everything except one value (m = 1, always returns the same mapped value). Likely follow-ups: prove uniformity (the mapping is a bijection from [0, m) onto the valid set), handle streaming/blacklist updates, or extend to weighted picks.
